title: Greenhouse Experiment
text:
Stipa pulchra Greenhouse Experiment
Spring quarter 2026 I interned with the Cheadle Center for Biodiversity and Ecological Restoration to help plan and begin a greenhouse experiment. The purpose of this experiment was to test Stipa pulchra survivorship in response to varying salinity levels. This experiment was done to investigate a hypothesis looking at why Stipa pulchra had seen die off at the North Campus Open Space restoration site in recent years. The experimental design included four salinity treatments with wet versus dry treatments for 80 individual plants.
My work in this project mainly involved the experimental design, data collection, salinity treatment, and creating preliminary visualizations for the data collected. My work on the project ended after spring quarter 2026, but the project continued after this. The figure below is a preliminary data visualization I created for the project. The figure caption was written by me for this website, and the visualization was done in R. Additional preliminary visualizations along with the original Quarto Documents are in the Elises_work folder on the project’s GitHub repository.


View code
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)
library(here)
# reading in files
leaf_count <- read.csv(here("data", "Stipa_salinity_experiment_data - survival_leaves_2026_05_27.csv")) |>
  
# cleaning data 

  # cleaning names 
  clean_names() |> 
  # selecting for desired columns
  select(
    water, 
    live_leaves,
    green_leaves, 
    salinity) |> 
  # remove rows with missing values (NAs) to keep the graph clean
  drop_na(live_leaves, green_leaves) |> 
  # calculating proportion of live leaves using mutate
  mutate(
    proportion_live = live_leaves / (live_leaves + green_leaves),
    salinity = as.factor(salinity)
  )

# creating preliminary visualization

# base layer 
ggplot(leaf_count,
       # looking at salinity on the x axis, proprtion_live on y axis
       # filling by treatment
       mapping = aes(x = salinity,
                     y = proportion_live,
                     fill = water)) +
  # first layer: geom_boxplot
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5,
               position = position_dodge(0.8)) +
  # second layer: geom_jitter
  geom_jitter(
    # coloring by treatment
    aes(color = water),
    # adjusting positioning and size
    position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.2, dodge.width = 0.8),
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 2,
    shape = 21
  ) +
  # adding title, subtitle, naming axes 
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Live Leaves by Salinity and Water Treatment",
    subtitle = "Data from 5/27/2026 and 5/28/2026",
    x = "Salinity Treatment (dS/m)",
    y = "Proportion of Live Leaves",
    fill = "Watering Treatment"
  ) +
  # adding theme
  theme_minimal() +
  # removing legend for readability
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  # adding custom colors for boxplot and jitter
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("wet" = "skyblue3", "dry" = "darkkhaki")
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("wet" = "skyblue3", "dry" = "darkkhaki")
  )









Proportion of Live Leaves by Salinity and Water Treatment: Wet treatments are indicated in blue; dry treatments in yellow. Individual observations are represented by points, with box plots displaying the median and interquartile range (IQR) for each treatment group. Data collected by Elise LaFreniere and Abriel Lau; visualization generated by Elise LaFreniere.

title: Film Photography
text:
I first started film photography when I was 15 years old on a point and shoot my parents got me for Christmas. I love capturing the world, my friends, and even myself through the lens of a camera. Featured in this map are photos taken on my Canon AE-1 on 35mm Kodak gold film.
Displayed is an interactive map showing locations where I have taken my photos. The map centers around Isla Vista but includes photos from Santa Barbara, Catalina Island, the bay, and New York.


Code
# loading in packages
library(leaflet)
library(tidyverse)

# creating object gps to store photo data 
gps <- read_csv("data/photo_gps_updated.csv")

# creating gps grouped data
gps_grouped <- gps |> 
  group_by(location, latitude, longitude) |> 
  summarize(
    # creating thumbnails 
    popup_content = paste0(
      '<div style="max-width: 280px; text-align: center;">',
        '<h4 style="margin: 0 0 10px 0; font-family: inherit; font-size: 14px;">', unique(location), '</h4>',
        '<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; justify-content: center;">',
          paste0(
          '<div style="text-align: center; width: 100%;">',
              '<a href="images/', filename, '" class="lightbox" data-gallery="map-gallery" title="', desc, '">',
                '<img src="images/', filename, '" style="width: 120px; height: 120px; object-fit: cover; border-radius: 4px; cursor: pointer; box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"/>',
              '</a>',
              '<p style="margin: 4px 0 0 0; font-size: 12px; color: #555; font-style: italic; max-width: 200px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">', desc, '</p>',
            '</div>',
            collapse = ""
          ),
        '</div>',
      '</div>'
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# generate the interactive map layout
site_map <- leaflet(data = gps_grouped) |>  
  
  # Add base map layers
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery, group = "ESRI World Imagery") |>  
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.OceanBasemap, group = "ESRI Oceans") |> 
  
  # add mini map
  addMiniMap(toggleDisplay = TRUE, minimized = TRUE) |> 
  
  # Center map at Isla Vista area
  setView(lng = -119.83, lat = 34.44, zoom = 10) |> 
  
# add location bubbles and markers 
  addMarkers(clusterOptions = markerClusterOptions(),
             lng = ~longitude, lat = ~latitude,
             popup = ~popup_content) |> 

  # add layers control 
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("ESRI World Imagery", "ESRI Oceans"))

# print map 
site_map

title: Research Assistant Work with Professor Bui
text:
Background
In Fall 2026, I began work as a research assistant for UCSB Professor, An Bui, and am earning course credit for this work through ENVS 199RA. My work involves finding, cleaning, and creating visualizations for data sets from the Santa Barbara Coastal LTER that demonstrate specific functions in R. These data sets and code will be used for Professor Bui’s winter course, ENVS 193DD. I will also be creating an infographic from SBC LTER data sets that match my ecological interests to develop my data visualization skills. This work is currently ongoing, and this page will be updated as it progresses.
Below is an example of a class data set using the mutate function. This work explores a laboratory experiment on urchin foraging rates (DiForne et al.). The full code and write up, along with additional work that is currently in progress are in the course GitHub repository.


Urchin Foraging Rates on Kelp at Different Urchin Densities

Set Up


View code
# loading in packages 
library(tidyverse) # general use
library(janitor) # cleaning data 
library(here) # data organization 

# reading in data 

# urchin density data from DiFiore et al. 2021
urchin <- read.csv(here("data","mesocosm_density_data copy.csv"))




Cleaning Data & Using Mutate Functions


View code
# create new object urchin_clean
urchin_clean <- urchin |> 
  # clean column names
  clean_names() |>
   # filter for trials with no mortality 
  filter(mortality == 0) |> 
  # mutate p_r to show the different species of urchins
  rename(species = p_r) |> 
  mutate(species = case_when(
    species == "p" ~ "Purple urchin",
    species == "r" ~ "Red urchin"
    )) |> 
  # grouping data for summarize
  group_by(trial_id, tank, species, urchin_density, total_time, kelp_in, kelp_out) |> 
  # using summarize to create urchin_biomass
  summarize(urchin_biomass = sum(urchin_mass)/1.587) |> 
  #ungrouping columns
  ungroup() |> 
  # mutate kelp_in and kelp_out columns to the kelp foraging rate of the urchins
   mutate(kelp_consumption_rate = ((kelp_in - kelp_out) / total_time)*24) |>
  mutate(rate_per_urchin = (kelp_consumption_rate) / urchin_density) |> 
  # select for desired columns of interest 
  select(urchin_density, rate_per_urchin, species, total_time, kelp_consumption_rate, urchin_biomass) 




Visualizations


View code
# base plot 
ggplot(data = urchin_clean,
  # x-axis urchin density, y-axis urchin consumption rate
  # color by species 
       mapping = aes(x = urchin_density,
                     y = rate_per_urchin,
                     color = species)) + 
  # first layer: geom_point
  geom_point(shape = 20,
             alpha = 0.5,
             size = 4) + 
  # separating by species 
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  # customizing colors
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Purple urchin" = "mediumorchid4",
    "Red urchin" = "firebrick")) +
  # labeling axes and adding title 
  labs(x = "Urchin density (per tank)",
       y = "Kelp consumed (gd^-1) per urchin",
       title = "Per-urchin foragaing rate on kelp \nacross different urchin densities") + 
  # adding custom theme 
  theme_minimal() +
  # removing legend
  theme(legend.position = "none")









This visualization shows the kelp foraging rate (gd-1) per urchin across different urchin densities, separated by urchin species. The red urchin data had fewer observations and were only tested at lower urchin densities than the purple urchin data. Comparing the two panels, the red urchins appear to have higher foraging rates per urchin at lower densities. Overall, foraging rates per urchin were highly variable, particularly at low urchin densities. For red urchins, the foraging rate per urchin appeared to decrease as density increased, yet for the purple urchins, there was no clear trend.


View code
# base plot 
ggplot(data = urchin_clean,
  # x-axis urchin density, y-axis urchin consumption rate
  # color by species 
       mapping = aes(x = urchin_biomass,
                     y = kelp_consumption_rate,
                     color = species)) + 
  # first layer: geom_point
  geom_point(shape = 20,
             alpha = 0.5,
             size = 4) + 
    # separating by species 
  facet_wrap(~species) +
    # customizing colors
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Purple urchin" = "mediumorchid4",
    "Red urchin" = "firebrick")) +
  labs(x = "Urchin biomass (gm^-2)",
       y = "Kelp consumption rate (gd^-1)",
       title = "Kelp consumption rate versus urchin biomass") + 
  # adding custom theme 
  theme_minimal() +
  # removing legend
  theme(legend.position = "none")









This visualization shows the kelp consumption rate (gd-1) across different urchin densities, separated by species. The red urchin data had fewer observations and were tested at lower urchin densities than the purple urchin data. In lower densities, kelp consumption rates appear to be similar across both species, though few red urchins had higher rates. Overall, kelp foraging rates appears to increase with increased urchin densities.


Data Citation
DiFiore, B, M. Rennick, J. Curtis, D. Reed, A. Stier. 2021. SBC LTER: Sea urchin foraging rates on giant kelp ver 1. Environmental Data Initiative. https://doi.org/10.6073/pasta/6af4cc3b0e63b887baf1ae9201e1cd1d. Accessed 2026-10-16.
